Japan’s steep climb for modernization also had large detriments environmentally and politically. This is especially noticeable when accounting for Meiji Japan’s imperialistic desires, due to their drive for resources and infrastructure; large-scale deforestation was carried out to fuel factories and railways which in turn caused devastating floods and crop failures (David Fedman, 2020). Most land was redistributed as well, especially arable land, but nationalizing woodlands disrupted traditional land-use. Even politically, Japan gradually regained sovereignty by finally revising unequal treaties in 1894, but it soon became an imperial power itself, following the Western path (Eijiro Honjo, 1932). This was primarily noticeable when Japan engaged in the Sino-Japanese War in 1894-1895 and Russo-Japanese War in 1904-1905 which gave Japan influence over Korea, Taiwan, and parts of China (Columbia Uni., 2025). In short, Japan escaped the grasp of Western rule only to reshape its surroundings by bringing in Japanese customs and bureaucrats into the colonized Korea and Hokkaido regions, which was all at the expense of the indigenous Ainu (Japanese indigenous people).

This poster’s intended audience is to all students interested in exploring creative opportunities. This addresses all students, not even just students, it makes opportunity feel unique and personal to you as the audience member. I think this argument also develops further through the comic-book design itself, the bright colors, lettering, and the different panels all tell a smaller part of the the story. A connection I had to this poster was how it brings out that imaginative curiosity I have without me realizing. I also think the art style builds on how the viewer perceives themselves as the main character in their own creative journey. Even the variety of careers illustrated reinforces my point of targeting all students, not just oregon state, suggesting their future is still unfolding and all students can shape themselves through opportunity. However, I can see how the poster doesn’t target professionals with a set career in place, as the questions asked “READY TO JOIN THE STORY?” implies that poster is intended for people looking to begin their careers over people who already have found one.

The text here immediately communicates urgency by treating financial hardships as this countdown rather than a distant issue. I see this through the language of the text within each statistic, quote, and paragraph, every point made establishes this deadline that all workers constantly face just to survive for the week. I think this argument develops better when I point out this bolded contradiction mentioned in the paragraph at the top right, "administration has increased by $161 million” and that being over the last ten years. This screams urgency, and mainly due to the attention brought on the numbers. While administrators spent nearly a decade to enforce change, workers still find themselves struggling to make through the next few weeks. I, as part of the audience, feel compelled and convinced on how urgent the matter is, as workers can’t afford to wait years for change. What I find interesting is how the flyer emphasizes the phrase ‘before the next paycheck’ rather than simply stating that workers are struggling financially. The word ‘before’ paints this scenario as a timeline, almost like a clock, in which something as routine as waiting for a payday becomes this race against time. When I think of payday, immediately what comes to mind is a sense of relief, but the flyer here reverse this feeling or expectation by showing how workers can’t even survive up until this point. I think what’s more critical about this is how it’s proposed as this never ending cycle rather than something that happens once. Especially when the flyer opens with “Why are we striking?”, this flyer reinforces that workers ARE taking action which communicates to the audience that this isn’t an issue waiting to happen, it already is at its breaking point.

The design of a toy is meant to appeal to children of all ages and entertain them. Toys are colorful, playful objects meant to evoke positive emotions and tap into the inner imagination of children. Yet entertainment is never culturally neutral. Even as toys invite play, they also communicate ideas about who matters, who belongs, and what kinds of identities and stories are valued. I will be examining the contemporary Disney Princess doll section, through the retail store, to argue that these toys shape how children interpret and understand gender and race rooted in colonial/imperialist history. While Disney makes an effort to market its princess line as inclusive and empowering, the toys continue to naturalize elements of whiteness, heteronormativity, and even able-bodied femininity. Referencing feminist and critical race perspectives, this essay argues that Disney princess toys function as these consumer-friendly stories about power and belonging. Through a feminist and intersectionalist analysis, this paper demonstrates how ascribed differences are socially constructed through toys and how these representations diverge from the lived experiences of real communities.

The racial dynamics of the Disney princesses toy section are subtle but persistent. What was most noticeable was how the white princesses tended to dominate the shelf space and the products sold, often appearing in mutiple variations and themed playsets. Princesses of colors were represented by typically in fewer variations, showcasing which type of characters are considered central and which are secondary. This imbalance really highlights how whiteness has become the default standard within the princess line.

The not so obvious persuasion that draws the audience while being hidden in the background is the spelling and placement of the name “JOHNATHAN!” relevant to the context of the prose. I found myself overlooking this detail multiple times after rereading the prose, until I realized what looked odd about this name. The misspelling of the name is a characteristic that soon caught my attention, the additional ‘h’ alone invites the audience to question whether the name is truly spelled that way or that is a misspelling. Now, the reason why I found this to be a genius, hidden way to persuade the audience was to do with the placement of the maybe misspelled name. It immediately gets you to question who is ‘Johnathan’ and do I know this person. When I say it gets you questioning who Johnathan is, I am referring to that little part of your brain that connects the context from the prose to the audiences’ memory to recollect if they recognize the person. This is the perfect example of persuasion, as it causes one to move to action, the audience shifts their thinking to immediately recollect whether their version of ‘Johnathan’ happens to match the context from this ‘Johnathan’. There is so much going on with this word that is also extremely effective in persuading the audience, however the following may be slightly more obvious. I started to notice after looking at the name a few times that the name serves two different purposes which only exist depending on which one purpose you notice first. One being to get the audeince to wonder whether they know a “Johnathan" and find out through the QR code, and the other making the audience eager to find out how ‘Johnathan’ messed up. The second purpose is equally as important as the first because the second shows that some of the viewers may not necessarily care about who ‘Johnathan’ is, but rather because they want to satisfy the questions the poster raised. I think this is what makes the simple misspelled name ‘Johnathan’ one of the most crucial parts of persuasion, and especially how subtly it is done.

At first glance, the Disney princess toy section appears colorful and varied, with there being characters from different films and worlds. However, just with a closer look, the section reveals a striking consistency in how these dolls are designed and marketed. The princess dolls are lined and grouped by franchise, being dressed with various gowns to be primarily marketed towards young girls. It becomes noticeable that despite representing many different films and cultural settings, the dolls themselves retain nearly identical features. Within this space it seems as if differences such as gender and race are presented as natural rather than them being socially constructed concepts. This idea is reinforced as in this section beauty and romance are heavily emphasized themes, far more than leadership or strength which seem to be nearly absent in the princess line. Even when racial diversity is present, such as with characters like Tiana, Jasmine, or Moana, all the dolls seem to follow this narrow standard of femininity. Julie Passante Elman claimed this focus to be categorized as Disney’s shift toward ‘capacity feminism,’([Elman](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14680777.2020.1855223)) which argues how Disney promotes a version of feminism that values women who are able-bodied and high achieving. This becomes more prevalent as nearly all the dolls have been restricted to slimmer bodies and delicate mannerisms; which underlines how these similarities in design do not feel coincidental. Instead, they suggest that while Disney may offer surface level diversity, there is still a very specific version of femininity that is promoted and treated as ideal. This actively communicates which bodies are seen as desirable and which remain on the margins.

Further evidence of ‘capacity feminism’ is explored through the specific marketing language Disney advertises their dolls. This shows up in the branding of ‘strong’ princesses who are still limited to the same physical and emotional expectations as earlier Disney adaptations. This is particularly seen in how disability and difference are non-existent, these Disney princesses fail to address non-normative gender expressions. There are no dolls or bodies that fall outside of thin, able-bodied norms. This brings rise to an issue that promotes the message to children how strength and worth are directly tied to looking a certain way, in short it connects physical perfection and appeal to one’s worth. Despite these dolls being marketed as empowering, this empowerment almost feels conditional, as if it is only reserved for those who fit within their specific boundaries.

Japan's industrial transformation during the Meiji period involved major environmental and political changes. Expanding railways and factories increased demand for timber and other resources, and extensive logging placed pressure on forests that communities had long relied on. Changes in land ownership further altered the ways that villagers could use and manage shared resources. At the same time, Japan sought to revise unequal treaties and strengthen its position in international affairs. Its growing influence also depended on imperial expansion. Military victories against China and Russia helped Japan extend its reach across East Asia, while policies in places such as Hokkaido and Korea brought local communities under Japanese institutions. For Indigenous Ainu communities, this process came with profound losses of autonomy and cultural recognition. Taken together, these changes show that the pursuit of modernization had uneven consequences. A state that worked to regain control over its foreign relations also used that power to constrain the choices of people living in territories it governed.

The study provides a useful overview of how the program developed and gives readers a clear way to follow its methods. Its participants came from a range of academic backgrounds, which helped the researchers gather perspectives beyond a single department. Following several cohorts also gave the program staff opportunities to review feedback between years and see whether their adjustments addressed earlier problems.

The submission describes the mentoring structure in considerable detail and makes a persuasive case for introducing students to microelectronics early. Its fit with an integrated-circuits conference is less direct. The authors could strengthen the connection by showing what students learned about circuit behavior, what tools they used, or how they assessed a design. The quantum computing component would also benefit from a specific example of a lab or exercise. As written, the paper's main contribution concerns the design of an undergraduate research experience. That is a valuable contribution, although it may be more immediately relevant to an engineering education audience.

The longitudinal design makes it possible to compare trends across cohorts, but the main measures rely on how students and mentors describe their experiences. A student can report greater confidence without demonstrating a corresponding improvement in technical skills. A short design task administered before and after the program could complement the surveys and provide a clearer comparison. The range of institutions, disciplines, and student backgrounds is an advantage. A subsequent study could use the same approach in another setting and report how the results change with different resources and mentoring arrangements.

The recruitment poster uses a comic-book layout to make creative careers feel accessible to a broad student audience. Its largest headline, “YOUR FUTURE AWAITS,” speaks directly to the reader and leaves the specific opportunity open until the viewer looks at the surrounding panels. Those panels show several kinds of work, which makes the message feel relevant to students who may have different interests or who have yet to settle on a career. The colors and expressive lettering also create movement across the page. Each panel offers a small glimpse of an activity, and together they suggest that there are many ways to take part. The question “READY TO JOIN THE STORY?” builds on this approach by inviting the reader to imagine taking the next step. It fits students exploring their options particularly well because the poster presents the future as something still being written. Someone established in a profession may appreciate the artwork, but the invitation is oriented toward people beginning to consider what they might do. That balance lets the poster reach beyond students already familiar with media work while giving its central audience a clear reason to pay attention.

The strike flyer makes financial pressure feel immediate by contrasting the timing of institutional spending with the timing of a worker's expenses. Its statement that spending on administration increased by $161 million over ten years gives the reader a long period to consider. Workers have a much shorter window. Bills arrive when they arrive, and the flyer emphasizes the difficulty of covering those costs before the next paycheck. That phrase changes the way the audience experiences the issue. It invites the reader to imagine counting the days left in an ordinary pay period and checking whether their money will last. A paycheck that should offer some breathing room becomes a deadline that must be reached. By placing that experience next to the decade-long spending figure, the flyer suggests that the institution has had years to make decisions while employees face the consequences in intervals of days or weeks. The heading “Why are we striking?” makes the purpose of this contrast clear. A strike is already underway, so the statistics help explain why the workers decided to act when they did. The flyer also presents the shortfall as recurring. Even a worker who manages to pay an urgent bill this week can face the same problem again soon. This combination of repetition and limited time gives the reader a concrete way to understand why a promise of gradual improvement may feel insufficient.

Finding a scholarly article on the discomfort caused by chalk sounds took longer. Researchers tend to discuss reactions to abrasive noises alongside other kinds of sound sensitivity, so a search focused only on classrooms missed much of that literature. Broader terms helped me find a source that addressed the experience I was looking for.

The Disney Princess display provides a useful example of how a familiar toy can communicate social expectations. Its bright packaging and recognizable characters invite children to imagine different stories, but the dolls also present a particular picture of beauty and success. Many of the figures share slim bodies, elaborate outfits, and similar poses. These repeated choices matter because children see them across characters with otherwise different backgrounds and adventures. Disney promotes some princesses through messages about independence and courage, yet the products still connect those qualities with a limited set of appearances. A feminist reading can examine how that combination shapes ideas about femininity. A critical race perspective adds questions about how much space different characters receive and whose stories are treated as central. Examining the figures alongside their packaging and placement helps show how expectations about gender and race are reinforced through ordinary retail decisions.

Differences in shelf space can reveal how a toy line treats its characters. In the Disney Princess section, several white princesses appear in multiple outfits and playsets, giving shoppers several ways to choose the same character. Princesses of color often appear in fewer versions. The display may look diverse as a whole, but the distribution of products gives some characters a more persistent presence than others.
